questions.stem: You are the ED intern seeing Jeff, 35, who has severe acute asthma after exposure to a cat and pollen. Salbutamol via spacer and oxygen have been started and the senior is on the way. You now have time for a few targeted questions. Which question best identifies his risk of a fatal asthma attack?
options: "How old were you when first diagnosed with asthma, and who made the diagnosis?"
"Does anyone in your family have asthma, eczema or hayfever?"
"Have you ever needed intensive care or a breathing tube for asthma?"
"Does exercise or cold air tend to make your breathing worse?"
questions.why: Previous ICU admission or intubation is the strongest marker of risk of a fatal attack. Ask it of every person with asthma, along with admissions, oral steroid courses, reliever use, preventer use and whether they have a written action plan.
notes: Age at diagnosis helps confirm asthma but does not predict whether an attack will be fatal.
Family history and atopy support the diagnosis of asthma but do not grade the risk of this attack.
Exercise and cold air are triggers. Knowing about them helps long-term control but does not show the risk of a fatal attack.

questions.stem: Jeff, 35, cannot finish sentences. RR 28, SpO2 92% on room air, HR 116. He took 2 puffs of his own salbutamol an hour ago with little benefit and can use a spacer. The ED nurse asks, "How much salbutamol, and how?" What do you prescribe?
options: 4 puffs via pMDI and spacer, repeated every 4 hours as needed
12 puffs via pMDI and spacer every 20 minutes for the first hour
2.5 mg nebulised once, then review the response in 4 hours
IV salbutamol infusion at 5 microgram/minute as first-line therapy
questions.why: In severe acute asthma in adults, the Australian Asthma Handbook advises salbutamol 100 microgram x 12 puffs via pMDI and spacer every 20 minutes for the first hour. Use 5 mg nebulised, driven by oxygen, if he cannot use a spacer. Then reassess and give it again as needed.
notes: 4 puffs every 4 hours is a dose for mild exacerbations or maintenance, far too little for a man who cannot finish sentences.
A single 2.5 mg nebule followed by a 4-hour wait is too small a dose and too long an interval for severe asthma, which needs repeated doses in the first hour.
IV salbutamol is not first-line. Inhaled salbutamol works as well with fewer adverse effects, and IV is kept for senior or ICU use in refractory cases.

questions.stem: Jeff's first venous gas, taken on room air, showed pH 7.46 and pCO2 33 mmHg. An hour later he is still wheezy and breathless with RR 30, now looks tired, and his repeat venous pCO2 is 44 mmHg. What best explains the rise in his pCO2?
options: Renal compensation for the earlier respiratory alkalosis, with bicarbonate retention
Better ventilation-perfusion matching after bronchodilator treatment
Extra CO2 production from salbutamol-related lactic acidosis
Falling alveolar ventilation as tiring muscles fail against air trapping
questions.why: Early in acute asthma, hypoxaemia and stimulation of airway receptors drive hyperventilation, so pCO2 should be low. A normal or rising pCO2 in a patient who is still breathless means alveolar ventilation is failing from exhaustion and severe obstruction. This is a life-threatening feature that needs ICU review.
notes: Renal compensation for respiratory alkalosis excretes bicarbonate over days. It does not raise pCO2, which is set by alveolar ventilation.
Better ventilation-perfusion matching would improve gas exchange and come with clinical improvement, not a rising pCO2 in a tiring patient.
Salbutamol can cause lactic acidosis, but the normal response is to breathe harder and lower pCO2, so a rising pCO2 still points to failing ventilation.

questions.stem: Examining Jeff, 35, in the ED, you see him sitting forward with his hands on his knees. Muscles at the side of his neck tighten with every breath in, and you report accessory muscle use. Which muscles, running from the cervical vertebrae to the first and second ribs, are lifting his upper rib cage?
options: Upper fibres of trapezius, from the occiput and nuchal ligament to the clavicle
questions.why: The scalenes arise from the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae. Anterior and middle scalene insert on the first rib and posterior scalene on the second. With sternocleidomastoid, they are the main accessory muscles of inspiration recruited in severe airflow obstruction.
notes: The infrahyoid muscles attach to the hyoid, thyroid cartilage, sternum and scapula. They depress the hyoid and larynx and do not insert on the ribs.
Platysma is a thin superficial muscle of facial expression (facial nerve) in the subcutaneous tissue. It does not attach to the ribs or lift the rib cage.
Upper trapezius attaches to the clavicle and scapula and elevates the shoulder girdle. It does not run from the cervical vertebrae to the first and second ribs.
